check: How the data were generated (from the task document)
finding: Audio is machine-generated: "cheap acoustic loggers were clipped to fire hydrants... and left overnight to record short clips," so amplitude values were not hand-entered. Metadata were assembled by people: crews chose which logger to use ("that's what we had in the shop," i.e., not random), pipe material most likely comes from asset records, and labels come from dig outcomes. Working assumptions (not stated in the task): each logger recorded one 5-second clip per site, likely a cost or device limit, so there is no repeat measurement to average; clip timing was effectively random, so recording time should be unrelated to leak status; and loggers were split in proportion across pipe types and assigned randomly within each pipe type ("what we had in the shop"), so A/B differences reflect the device, not the site. Still unknown: how the 6 dug sites were chosen.
Problems: none. Note that the two pipe codes use different styles ("cast_iron" vs. "PVC"); both match the documentation.

check: Dug-site leak share vs. the 1-in-8 benchmark
finding: 3 of 6 dug sites leaked (50%) vs. 12.5% historically. Chance of 3+ leaks in 6 randomly chosen sites: 2.9%. The dug sites were almost certainly chosen because they seemed suspicious, so they over-represent leaks; any probabilities learned from them must be re-anchored to 1 in 8.
